title: Networking Fundamentals: How Networks and the Internet Work
subtitle: Understand how data crosses networks and the internet, from cables and switches to IP, TCP and DNS, and troubleshoot a connection yourself.
outcomes: Describe what networks are made of, from endpoints, switches and routers to access points and firewalls, and how they're cabled
Explain how data is wrapped and delivered, using the OSI and TCP/IP models, Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
Explain how IP addresses, subnet masks and default gateways get packets from one network to another
Compare TCP and UDP, and follow DNS and HTTP through the loading of a web page
Build and test small networks in Cisco Packet Tracer, and watch real traffic in Wireshark
Troubleshoot a connection step by step with ping, traceroute and tracert, and ipconfig or ip
prerequisites: None: this course starts from zero. You need a Windows, macOS or Linux computer that can run Cisco Packet Tracer (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account) and Wireshark (free from wireshark.org), and that you're allowed to install software and capture traffic on.
description:
How does a message get from your laptop to a server on the other side of the world, and what do you check when it doesn't? This course explains how networks and the internet work, from the cables and switches in a building to the addresses, protocols and names that carry a web page to your screen. You'll meet the devices networks are made of, the OSI and TCP/IP models, Ethernet and MAC addresses, IP addresses and default gateways, TCP, UDP and ports, and what DNS and HTTP do when a page loads.

You'll learn it hands-on. You'll build networks in Cisco Packet Tracer and step through them packet by packet in Simulation mode, look inside real frames with Wireshark, and test your own computer's connection with ping, traceroute and ipconfig or ip. Every module ends with a lab your instructor reviews, and the course ends with a project in which you build, test and document a network end to end. The course follows the Network Fundamentals section of Cisco's published CCNA (200-301) exam topics, making it a good first step towards that exam.
aligned_with: Cisco CCNA (200-301) exam topics: Network Fundamentals

modules.title: What networks are made of
modules.summary: Meet the devices a network is built from, the shapes networks are built in and the cables that join them, then build your first network in Cisco Packet Tracer.

lessons.title: Endpoints, switches, routers and the rest
objectives: Describe the job of endpoints, servers, switches, routers, access points and firewalls
Explain the difference between a LAN, a WAN and the internet
key_points: A network connects devices so they can share data. Endpoints, also called hosts, such as laptops, phones, printers and cameras, send and receive it; servers are hosts that provide services, such as web pages or files, to clients.
A switch joins the devices within one local network (LAN). It forwards each Ethernet frame only to the port where its destination MAC address is, so it works mainly at layer 2.

A router joins different networks and forwards packets between them by their destination IP address, at layer 3. A home router usually combines a router, a switch, a wireless access point and a firewall in one box.

A wireless access point (AP) connects Wi-Fi devices to the wired network; the network's Wi-Fi name is its SSID. APs, IP phones and cameras are often powered over their network cable by the switch, with Power over Ethernet (PoE).

A firewall decides which traffic may pass between networks, by rules about addresses, ports and applications; next-generation firewalls and intrusion prevention systems (IPS) also inspect traffic for known attacks.
A LAN covers one site, such as a home, office or campus; a WAN links sites across long distances; and the internet is a global network of networks run by many different organisations.

walkthrough.title: Find your way around Packet Tracer

steps.do: Open Cisco Packet Tracer and sign in with your Cisco Networking Academy account. The large white area is the Logical workspace, where you build networks.
Look at the bottom-left corner: the top row picks a category, such as Network Devices or End Devices, the row below picks a type, such as Routers or Switches, and the models appear beside them.
Drag a 2911 router (Network Devices > Routers), a 2960 switch (Network Devices > Switches), a PC and a Server (End Devices) into the workspace.
steps.see: Each device appears with its model and a name, such as 2911 Router0 and PC-PT PC0.

steps.do: Click the router. The Physical tab shows the device itself, Config has forms for common settings, and CLI is the Cisco IOS command line you'll use in later courses. Close the window.
Click the PC. Its Desktop tab holds the tools a user would have, such as IP Configuration, Command Prompt and Web Browser.
Rest the pointer on the router for a moment.
steps.see: A summary of its ports, whether each link is up, and their addresses.

steps.do: Find the Realtime and Simulation tabs at the bottom right. Realtime runs the network at normal speed; Simulation steps through traffic packet by packet, which this course uses often.
Save the file with File > Save As. Packet Tracer files end in .pkt.

lessons.title: Network topologies and designs
objectives: Distinguish physical and logical topologies, and star, mesh and point-to-point layouts
Describe common designs: SOHO, two-tier and three-tier campus, spine-leaf, WAN and cloud
key_points: A physical topology is how devices are actually cabled and where they are; a logical topology is how data flows between them, such as which devices share a network.

Ethernet LANs use a star: every device has its own cable to a switch, and joining switches to each other makes an extended star. A full mesh links every device to every other for resilience; a partial mesh links only some.
A small office or home office (SOHO) network often relies on one small router that is also its switch, access point and firewall, with a link to an internet service provider.

Campus networks are built in layers: access switches connect users and devices, distribution switches join the access switches and apply policy, and a core moves traffic quickly between them. A two-tier (collapsed core) design merges distribution and core.
Data centres often use spine-leaf: servers connect to leaf switches, and every leaf links to every spine switch, so any two servers are the same number of hops apart.

Services can run on-premises, on equipment an organisation owns and runs itself, or in the cloud, on a provider's equipment reached over the internet or a private WAN link; many organisations use both.

lessons.title: Cables, connectors and interface problems
objectives: Compare copper and fibre cabling and choose the right cable for a link
Recognise interface problems such as duplex mismatches, speed mismatches and CRC errors
key_points: Most LAN cabling is unshielded twisted pair (UTP) copper with RJ-45 connectors, in categories such as Cat 5e and Cat 6; Ethernet over twisted pair reaches up to 100 metres.

A straight-through cable joins unlike devices, such as a PC and a switch; a crossover cable joins like devices, such as two switches. Most modern interfaces support auto-MDIX, which detects the cable and adjusts, so either kind works.

Fibre-optic cable carries light, so electrical interference doesn't affect it and it reaches much further than copper. Multimode fibre suits shorter runs inside buildings; single-mode fibre, with a much thinner core, carries laser light for many kilometres.

Today's Ethernet links are point-to-point and full duplex: each switch port has its own link and can send and receive at once. Old hubs made a shared, half-duplex medium where devices took turns and frames could collide.

Both ends of a link must agree on speed and duplex, which autonegotiation normally arranges. A duplex mismatch gives a slow link with collisions and errors; a speed mismatch usually stops the link from coming up at all.

show interfaces on a Cisco device reports a link's speed, duplex and error counters: rising input and CRC errors usually mean a damaged cable, a bad connector or interference, and late collisions point to a duplex mismatch.

walkthrough.title: Choose cables and read an interface's health

steps.do: In a new file, add a 2911 router, a 2960 switch and a PC. Open Connections (the lightning bolt) at the bottom left and rest the pointer on each cable to see its name.
steps.see: Automatically Choose Connection Type, Console, Copper Straight-Through, Copper Cross-Over, Fiber and more.

steps.do: Choose Copper Straight-Through, click the PC and choose FastEthernet0, then click the switch and choose FastEthernet0/1.
steps.see: A cable with a light at each end. The switch's light is amber at first and turns green after about 30 seconds, once the port starts forwarding.

steps.do: Connect the switch's GigabitEthernet0/1 to the router's GigabitEthernet0/0 with another Copper Straight-Through cable.
steps.see: Red lights: a router's interfaces stay shut down until you turn them on.

steps.do: Click the router and open its CLI tab. If it asks Would you like to enter the initial configuration dialog?, type no and press Enter. Then turn the interface on.
steps.code:
enable
configure terminal
interface g0/0
no shutdown
end
steps.see: %LINK-5-CHANGED: Interface GigabitEthernet0/0, changed state to up, and the lights turn green.

steps.do: Read the interface's health.
steps.see: GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up, then lines with its duplex and speed, such as Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, and counters such as 0 input errors, 0 CRC and 0 late collision.

steps.do: When you're not sure which cable two devices need, use Automatically Choose Connection Type: Packet Tracer picks the right one. Real networks rely on auto-MDIX for the same convenience.

lab.title: Build and test your first network
lab.goal: Build a small LAN in Packet Tracer, a switch and three PCs, give each PC an IP address and show that every PC can reach the others.
setup: Cisco Packet Tracer installed and signed in (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account)

steps.do: In a new file, add a 2960 switch (Network Devices > Switches) and three PCs (End Devices).
Connect PC0, PC1 and PC2 to the switch's FastEthernet0/1, 0/2 and 0/3 with Copper Straight-Through cables, and wait until every light is green.
On PC0, open Desktop > IP Configuration, keep Static, type the IPv4 Address 192.168.1.10 and click in the Subnet Mask box.
steps.see: Packet Tracer fills in 255.255.255.0 for you.

steps.do: Give PC1 192.168.1.11 and PC2 192.168.1.12, each with the mask 255.255.255.0. Leave Default Gateway empty: these PCs only talk to each other.
On PC0, open Desktop > Command Prompt and ping the other two PCs.
steps.see: Reply from 192.168.1.11: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=128, four times. The very first reply can be Request timed out. while the PCs learn each other's MAC addresses; ping again and all four reply.

steps.do: Check PC0's settings from its command line.
steps.see: IPv4 Address: 192.168.1.10 and Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0.

steps.do: Break it on purpose: change PC2's address to 192.168.2.12, keeping the same mask, and ping it from PC0.
steps.see: Request timed out. four times.

steps.do: Put PC2 back to 192.168.1.12, ping it once more to confirm, and save the file as first-lan.pkt: the next module uses it.

checks.text: PC0 has the right address and mask.
The learner explains that at 192.168.2.12, PC2 was on a different network from PC0, and that without a router between them they can't talk.

lab.submit: Paste the output of both pings and of ipconfig from PC0's Command Prompt, then a sentence or two explaining why PC0 couldn't reach PC2 at 192.168.2.12.
hints: If a ping fails, rest the pointer on each PC to check its address, and make sure every link light is green.
Plug each PC's FastEthernet0 port into a numbered FastEthernet port on the switch, not the Console port.

modules.title: Layers, Ethernet and switching
modules.summary: See how data is wrapped in layers on its way across a network, what's inside an Ethernet frame, and how a switch learns where every device is.

lessons.title: The OSI and TCP/IP models
objectives: Name the seven OSI layers and the four TCP/IP layers, and what each does
Explain encapsulation and the name of the data unit at each layer
key_points: The OSI model describes networking in seven layers: 7 application, 6 presentation, 5 session, 4 transport, 3 network, 2 data link and 1 physical. Each layer uses the service of the layer below and serves the one above.
The TCP/IP model, which the internet is built on, has four layers: application (OSI layers 5 to 7), transport (layer 4), internet (layer 3) and network access, also called link (layers 1 and 2).

On the way down, each layer adds its own header to what it was given: this is encapsulation. Application data becomes a segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP) at the transport layer, a packet at the network layer, a frame at the data link layer, and bits on the wire.
The receiver reverses the process, de-encapsulation: each layer reads and removes its own header and passes the rest up, until the application has the original data.

Devices are often described by the highest layer they work at: cables and hubs at layer 1, switches at layer 2 with MAC addresses, routers at layer 3 with IP addresses, and applications such as web browsers at layer 7.
Layers make troubleshooting easier: working from the bottom up, from cables and link lights to addresses to applications, narrows a problem down to one layer.

steps.do: Open first-lan.pkt from the module 1 lab and click the Simulation tab at the bottom right.
steps.see: The Simulation Panel opens, with an empty Event List.

steps.do: Under Event List Filters, click Edit Filters and, on the IPv4 tab, tick only ARP and ICMP, so the list shows just those protocols.
Choose Add Simple PDU (the closed envelope in the toolbar), then click PC0 and then PC2.
steps.see: An envelope waits on PC0.

steps.do: Click Capture/Forward to move one step at a time and watch the envelopes.
steps.see: First ARP envelopes, as PC0 asks for PC2's MAC address, then ICMP envelopes travelling between PC0 and PC2.

steps.do: Click an ICMP envelope on PC0 to open its PDU Information window. The OSI Model tab lists the layers PC0 used, with what it did at each.
steps.see: Layer 3 with the source IP 192.168.1.10 and destination IP 192.168.1.12, Layer 2 with the Ethernet II header and its two MAC addresses, and Layer 1 with the port it leaves by.

steps.do: Open the Outbound PDU Details tab to see each header's fields laid out, from the Ethernet II frame to the ICMP message inside the IP packet.
Click an envelope at the switch. Its OSI Model tab goes up only to layer 2: a switch reads the frame's MAC addresses and doesn't need the IP packet inside.
Click the Realtime tab to go back to normal speed.

lessons.title: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
objectives: Describe the fields of an Ethernet frame and what each is for
Find and read MAC addresses, including the broadcast address
key_points: A MAC address is 48 bits, written as 12 hexadecimal digits such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E, 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E or, on Cisco devices, 001a.2b3c.4d5e. It identifies a network interface on the local network.

The first 24 bits of a MAC address are the OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier), which identifies the manufacturer, and the manufacturer assigns the rest. Many phones and laptops now use a random, private MAC address on Wi-Fi.

An Ethernet II frame holds the destination MAC address, the source MAC address, an EtherType that says what's inside (0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP), the data, and a frame check sequence (FCS) that lets the receiver detect damage.
The data in a standard Ethernet frame is 46 to 1500 bytes, so a frame, counting its header and FCS, is 64 to 1518 bytes; 1500 bytes is the usual MTU, the biggest packet a link carries.
A frame can be unicast, to one interface; broadcast, to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, which every device on the LAN receives; or multicast, to a group of devices that have asked for it.

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) finds the MAC address for an IPv4 address on the local network: a host broadcasts a request such as Who has 192.168.1.12?, that device replies with its MAC address, and the host keeps the answer in its ARP cache.

steps.do: Open Wireshark. The welcome screen lists interfaces; choose the one your computer uses now (Wi-Fi or Ethernet on Windows, en0 on most Macs, a name such as wlan0 or enp0s3 on Linux). Its sparkline moves when there's traffic. Capture only on a network you own or are allowed to monitor.
Start capturing: double-click the interface, or select it and start a capture.
In a terminal, find your default gateway (your router) and ping it.
steps.code:
# Windows: find Default Gateway, then ping it
ipconfig
ping 192.168.1.1

# macOS
route -n get default
ping -c 4 192.168.1.1

# Linux: the address after default via
ip route
ping -c 4 192.168.1.1
steps.see: Replies from your gateway. Use your own gateway's address in place of 192.168.1.1.

steps.do: Stop the capture.
Type arp in the display filter bar and press Enter.
steps.see: Requests such as Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.20 and replies such as 192.168.1.1 is at followed by a MAC address. If there are none, your computer already knew the address: clear the filter and use any packet.

steps.do: Select a packet, then in the packet details pane select Ethernet II and expand it.
steps.see: Destination, Source and Type, such as Type: IPv4 (0x0800) for a ping or Type: ARP (0x0806) for ARP.

steps.do: Look at an ARP request's Destination: Broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff). Wireshark shows the manufacturer's name in front of many source addresses, worked out from the OUI; a random, private address shows none.
Compare with your own MAC address: ipconfig /all on Windows (Physical Address), ifconfig en0 on macOS (ether), ip link on Linux (link/ether).

lessons.title: How switches learn, flood and forward
objectives: Explain how a switch builds its MAC address table
Predict whether a switch will forward, flood or filter a frame
key_points: A switch learns by reading the source MAC address of every frame it receives and recording it, with the port the frame arrived on, in its MAC address table.
For each frame it looks up the destination MAC address: if the address is in the table, the frame goes out of that one port; if that's the port it came in on, the frame is dropped (filtered).

Frames to unknown unicast addresses, and broadcast frames, are flooded: sent out of every port in the same VLAN except the one they arrived on. Multicast frames are flooded too, unless the switch has been set up to track who wants them.
Learned entries age out when no frames have come from that address for a while, 300 seconds by default on Cisco switches, so the table keeps up when devices move or leave.

Every switch port is its own collision domain, but all the ports in a VLAN share one broadcast domain: a broadcast reaches every device in it. Routers don't forward broadcasts, so they separate broadcast domains.
show mac address-table on a Cisco switch lists each address with its VLAN, its type (DYNAMIC if learned, STATIC if configured) and its port.

walkthrough.title: Watch a switch fill its MAC address table

steps.do: Open first-lan.pkt, click the switch and open its CLI tab. Press Enter to get the Switch> prompt, then enter privileged EXEC mode.
steps.see: The prompt changes from Switch> to Switch#.

steps.do: Empty the learned part of the table, so you can watch it fill.
steps.code:
clear mac address-table dynamic
show mac address-table
steps.see: Only the headings: Vlan, Mac Address, Type and Ports.

steps.do: On PC0's Command Prompt, ping PC1 (192.168.1.11). Then show the table again.
steps.see: Two DYNAMIC entries in VLAN 1: PC0's MAC address on Fa0/1 and PC1's on Fa0/2. PC2 isn't there: it received the ARP broadcast but hasn't sent anything.

steps.do: Ping PC2 from PC0 and show the table once more.
steps.see: Three entries, one per PC, each on its own port.

steps.do: Match the entries to the PCs: on each PC, run ipconfig /all and read its Physical Address.
On PC0, show its ARP cache.
steps.see: Internet Address, Physical Address and Type columns, with dynamic entries for 192.168.1.11 and 192.168.1.12.

lab.title: Watch a switch learn and flood
lab.goal: Use Simulation mode and the switch's command line to show how a switch floods an ARP broadcast, learns where each PC is, and then forwards frames out of one port only.
setup: Your first-lan.pkt from the module 1 lab, or the same network rebuilt: a 2960 switch and three PCs, 192.168.1.10, .11 and .12 with mask 255.255.255.0, on Fa0/1 to Fa0/3

steps.do: Open first-lan.pkt. On the switch's CLI, empty the learned addresses.
steps.code:
enable
clear mac address-table dynamic
show mac address-table
steps.see: Only the table's headings.

steps.do: On each PC's Command Prompt, empty the ARP cache, then check it.
steps.see: No ARP Entries Found. (If arp -d isn't accepted, save, close and reopen the file instead.)

steps.do: Click the Simulation tab. In Edit Filters, on the IPv4 tab, tick only ARP and ICMP.
With Add Simple PDU, click PC0 and then PC2. Use the Inspect tool (the magnifying glass) on the switch and choose MAC Table, and keep that window open.
Click Capture/Forward one step at a time until the ARP request has left the switch. Note which devices it goes to.
steps.see: The switch floods the request to PC1 and PC2. PC1 ignores it, as it isn't asking for PC1's address; PC2 answers.

steps.do: Keep stepping until the ping's reply reaches PC0, watching the MAC table window and where each frame goes.
steps.see: PC2's ARP reply and the ICMP echo request and reply each go out of one port only, and the table gains an entry each time a new source is seen.

steps.do: Click the Realtime tab. On the switch's CLI, show the table.
steps.see: Two DYNAMIC entries: PC0 on Fa0/1 and PC2 on Fa0/3. PC1 isn't listed, because it hasn't sent a frame.

steps.do: On PC0, show its ARP cache.
steps.see: One dynamic entry: 192.168.1.12 with PC2's MAC address.

steps.do: Now ping PC1 from PC0 in Realtime mode and show the switch's table once more.
steps.see: A third entry: PC1 on Fa0/2.

checks.text: After PC0 pinged PC2, the table held only PC0 (Fa0/1) and PC2 (Fa0/3), both DYNAMIC.
After PC0 pinged PC1, all three PCs appear, each on its own port.
PC0's ARP cache maps 192.168.1.12 to PC2's MAC address.

The learner explains that the ARP request was a broadcast, so the switch flooded it to every other port, while the replies and pings went out of one port because the switch had learned the destination.

lab.submit: Paste the switch's show mac address-table output after PC0 pinged PC2 and again after it pinged PC1, PC0's arp -a output, and a few sentences on what you saw in Simulation mode: where the ARP request went, where the reply and the pings went, and why.
hints: If PC1 appears in the table after the first ping, something made PC1 send a frame: empty the table and try again without touching PC1.
In Simulation mode the switch only learns as you step: keep clicking Capture/Forward until the reply reaches PC0.

modules.title: IP, transport and applications
modules.summary: Follow a packet from one network to another through a default gateway, see how TCP and UDP deliver data to the right application, and trace DNS and HTTP as a web page loads.

lessons.title: IP addresses, subnet masks and default gateways
objectives: Explain what an IPv4 address and subnet mask tell a device
Explain when a host sends a packet straight to its destination and when it uses its default gateway
key_points: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, such as 192.168.1.10. Part of it identifies the network and the rest identifies the host on that network.
The subnet mask says where the split falls: 255.255.255.0, also written /24, means the first 24 bits are the network, so 192.168.1.10/24 is a host on network 192.168.1.0.
Before sending, a host compares the destination's network with its own. If they match, it delivers the packet directly, using ARP to find the destination's MAC address.

If the destination is on another network, the host sends the packet to its default gateway, a router on its own network, using ARP to find the router's MAC address; the router then forwards it towards the destination.
The default gateway must be an address on the host's own network. Without one, a host can reach its own LAN but nothing beyond it, including the internet.
Most hosts get their address, mask, default gateway and DNS servers automatically from DHCP. IPv6 addresses, 128 bits written in hexadecimal, run alongside IPv4 on most networks today.

walkthrough.title: Connect two networks with a router

steps.do: In a new file, add a 2911 router, two 2960 switches and two PCs. With Copper Straight-Through cables, connect PC0 to Switch0 Fa0/1 and Switch0 Gig0/1 to the router's GigabitEthernet0/0, then PC1 to Switch1 Fa0/1 and Switch1 Gig0/1 to the router's GigabitEthernet0/1.
On the router's CLI, answer no to the initial configuration dialog, then give each interface an address on its own network and turn it on.
steps.code:
enable
configure terminal
interface g0/0
ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
interface g0/1
ip address 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
end

steps.do: Check both interfaces.
steps.see: GigabitEthernet0/0 with 192.168.1.1 and GigabitEthernet0/1 with 192.168.2.1, both with Status up and Protocol up.

steps.do: Give PC0 192.168.1.10, mask 255.255.255.0, and leave its Default Gateway empty for now. Give PC1 192.168.2.10, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.2.1.
From PC0, ping its router, then PC1.
steps.see: The router replies (TTL=255), but PC1 doesn't: PC0 has nowhere to send traffic for another network.

steps.do: Set PC0's Default Gateway to 192.168.1.1 and ping PC1 again.
steps.see: Reply from 192.168.2.10: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=127. PC1 sent the reply with a TTL of 128 and the router took one off as it forwarded it.

steps.do: Trace the path.
steps.see: Two hops: 192.168.1.1, the gateway, then 192.168.2.10.

steps.do: See how the router knows the two networks.
steps.see: C 192.168.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0 and C 192.168.2.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1, each with an L (local) route for the router's own address.

steps.do: Save the file as two-networks.pkt for the module's lab.

lessons.title: TCP, UDP and port numbers
objectives: Compare TCP and UDP and say which applications use each
Explain how port numbers deliver data to the right application
key_points: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it opens a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers the bytes it sends, resends anything lost, delivers data in order, and slows down when the receiver or the network can't keep up.

UDP is connectionless: it sends datagrams with no handshake, acknowledgements or resending, so it adds less overhead and delay. DNS lookups, DHCP, voice and video calls and many games use it, and cope with losses themselves.

Port numbers, from 0 to 65535, say which application a segment is for. Servers listen on well-known ports (0 to 1023), and a client uses a temporary port for each connection, often from 49152 to 65535.
Common ports: 20 and 21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67 and 68 DHCP, 69 TFTP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 123 NTP, 143 IMAP, 161 SNMP and 443 HTTPS.
A connection is identified by its two sockets, each an IP address plus a port, such as 192.168.1.20:51734 to 203.0.113.10:443, so one computer can hold many connections to the same server at once.
TCP closes a connection gracefully with a FIN from each side, or abruptly with a RST (reset), which is also the answer when nothing is listening on a TCP port.

walkthrough.title: See your computer's connections and ports

steps.do: Open a web page or two in your browser, then open a terminal: Command Prompt on Windows, Terminal on macOS or Linux.
List your TCP connections, with addresses and ports shown as numbers.
steps.code:
# Windows and macOS
netstat -an -p tcp

# Linux
ss -tan
steps.see: Lines with your address and a high port number, the server's address and port 443 (HTTPS), and a state such as ESTABLISHED. macOS shows the port after a final dot, as in 192.168.1.20.51734.

steps.do: Show only the connections that are established.
steps.code:
# Windows
netstat -an | findstr ESTABLISHED

# macOS
netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED

# Linux
ss -tn state established

steps.do: See which ports your computer listens on, waiting for connections.
steps.code:
# Windows
netstat -an | findstr LISTENING

# macOS
netstat -an | grep LISTEN

# Linux
ss -tln
steps.see: Ports your computer offers, some only to itself on 127.0.0.1.

steps.do: List UDP sockets too. UDP has no connections, so there's no state to read.
steps.code:
# Windows and macOS
netstat -an -p udp

# Linux
ss -uan

steps.do: To see which program owns each connection: netstat -b in a Command Prompt run as administrator on Windows, lsof -i -P on macOS, or ss -tnp on Linux (with sudo to see other users' programs).

lessons.title: DNS and HTTP: loading a web page
objectives: Describe how DNS turns a name into an IP address
Put the steps of loading a web page in order, from the DNS lookup to the HTTP response
key_points: DNS (Domain Name System) turns names such as www.example.com into IP addresses. A host asks its configured DNS server, a recursive resolver, usually over UDP port 53; large answers and transfers between servers use TCP port 53.

If the resolver hasn't cached the answer, it asks down the hierarchy: a root server points to the servers for the top-level domain (such as .com), which point to the domain's authoritative servers, which answer. Each answer has a TTL saying how long it may be cached.
Common DNS records: A (a name's IPv4 address), AAAA (its IPv6 address), CNAME (an alias for another name), MX (the domain's mail servers) and NS (its name servers).

To load https://www.example.com, the browser gets the address from DNS, opens a TCP connection to port 443 with the three-way handshake, sets up encryption with a TLS handshake, then sends an HTTP GET request; the server replies with a status code and the page.

HTTP status codes are grouped by their first digit: 2xx success (200 OK), 3xx redirection (301 Moved Permanently), 4xx client errors (403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found) and 5xx server errors (500 Internal Server Error).

HTTP on port 80 travels as readable text that anyone on the path could read or change; HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS, usually on port 443, which encrypts it and proves the server's identity with a certificate. One page usually leads to many more requests for images, scripts and styles.

walkthrough.title: Look up a name and fetch a page by hand

steps.do: Ask your DNS server for a name's address.
steps.see: Server and Address lines for the server that answered, then Non-authoritative answer: and the name with its addresses. Non-authoritative means the answer came from your resolver, not from the domain's own servers.

steps.do: Ask for its IPv6 address (the AAAA record) and its name servers (NS).
Fetch the page over plain HTTP and show only the response's headers. On Windows, type curl.exe, so that PowerShell doesn't run a different command of its own.
steps.see: A status line such as HTTP/1.1 200 OK, then headers such as Content-Type: text/html.

steps.do: Fetch it over HTTPS and show the whole conversation, saving the page itself to a file.
steps.see: Lines starting * are curl's notes, such as the address and port 443 it connected to and the TLS version; lines starting > are the request it sent (GET / followed by the HTTP version); lines starting < are the response.

steps.do: Ask for a page that doesn't exist and read the status code.
steps.see: A 4xx status, such as 404, meaning the client asked for something the server doesn't have.

steps.do: Empty your computer's DNS cache, so the next lookup goes to the server again: ipconfig /flushdns on Windows, sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder on macOS, or resolvectl flush-caches on Linux systems that use systemd-resolved.

lab.title: Follow a web page request in Packet Tracer
lab.goal: Add a DNS server and a web server to a two-network Packet Tracer lab, browse to the site by name, and use Simulation mode to put DNS, TCP and HTTP in the order they happen.
setup: Your two-networks.pkt from the walkthrough, or the same network rebuilt: a 2911 router with 192.168.1.1/24 on G0/0 and 192.168.2.1/24 on G0/1, a switch on each, and PC0 at 192.168.1.10 with gateway 192.168.1.1

steps.do: Open two-networks.pkt and delete PC1. Add two servers (End Devices > Server) to the switch on the 192.168.2.0 network.
In each server's Desktop > IP Configuration, set Server0 to 192.168.2.53 and Server1 to 192.168.2.80, both with mask 255.255.255.0 and default gateway 192.168.2.1.
On Server1, open Services > HTTP, keep HTTP and HTTPS on, and edit index.html: replace its text with the single line Hello from the lab web server, then save it.
On Server0, open Services > DNS, turn DNS Service On, and add an A Record with Name www.netlab.test and Address 192.168.2.80.
On PC0, open Desktop > IP Configuration and set DNS Server to 192.168.2.53.
Click the Simulation tab. In Edit Filters, on the IPv4 tab, tick only DNS, TCP and HTTP.

On PC0, open Desktop > Web Browser, type http://www.netlab.test and click Go. Then click Capture/Forward one step at a time until the page appears, writing down each event: its protocol, where it goes and what it does.
steps.see: DNS first (PC0's query to 192.168.2.53 and the answer), then TCP setting up a connection with 192.168.2.80, then HTTP: the request and the page coming back.

steps.do: Click the first DNS event's envelope and open its OSI Model tab. Find the layer 4 protocol and ports.
steps.see: UDP, with destination port 53.

steps.do: Click the first TCP event's envelope and find its ports.
steps.see: Destination port 80, the web server's HTTP port. This is the first segment of TCP's three-way handshake.

steps.do: Click the Realtime tab. On PC0's Command Prompt, look the name up.
steps.see: The server's address, 192.168.2.53, then Name: www.netlab.test and Address: 192.168.2.80.

steps.do: Save the file as web-lab.pkt.

checks.text: The name resolves to the web server's address.
The browser shows the edited page.
look_for: Hello from the lab web server

checks.text: The events are in the right order: the DNS query and answer, then the TCP handshake, then the HTTP request and response.
DNS is identified as UDP to port 53, and the web request as TCP to port 80.

lab.submit: Paste PC0's nslookup output, the text the browser showed, your numbered list of Simulation events from the DNS query to the page arriving (protocol, from, to and purpose), and the transport protocol and port you found for DNS and for HTTP.
hints: If the browser says it can't find the host, check PC0's DNS Server setting and that DNS Service is On, with the record added, on Server0.
If no DNS events appear, PC0 may have reused an earlier answer: add a second A Record, such as web.netlab.test for 192.168.2.80, and browse to the new name.

modules.title: Troubleshooting connectivity
modules.summary: Find out why something can't connect, methodically: check a computer's IP settings, test the path with ping and traceroute, and watch the tests themselves in Wireshark.

lessons.title: A method for troubleshooting
objectives: Apply a structured method to a network problem instead of guessing
Choose a bottom-up, top-down or divide-and-conquer approach
key_points: Good troubleshooting follows a method: define the problem precisely, gather information, form a theory of the cause, test it, fix it, check that the fix worked, and write down what you found and did.

Bottom-up starts at the physical layer, with cables, link lights and Wi-Fi signal, and works upwards; top-down starts at the application; divide-and-conquer starts in the middle, often with a ping, and moves up or down depending on the result.

A sensible order for a host that can't connect: is its link up; does it have an IP address, mask and default gateway; can it ping its gateway; can it reach a remote address by IP; and does DNS turn names into addresses?
Comparing with something that works narrows a problem: if one PC fails and its neighbour works, look at what's different about the failing PC, its cable, its switch port or its settings.
Change one thing at a time and test after each change, so you know what fixed the problem, and undo changes that didn't help.

Common causes: an unplugged or damaged cable, a wrong address, mask or gateway, a duplicate IP address, no answer from DHCP (shown on Windows by a 169.254 address), a DNS failure, or a firewall blocking the traffic.

lessons.title: Testing the path: ping and traceroute
objectives: Use ping to test reachability and read its results
Use traceroute or tracert to find where along a path traffic stops
key_points: ping sends ICMP echo requests (type 8) and waits for echo replies (type 0), reporting each round-trip time and how many were lost. A reply proves the path works in both directions.

Request timed out means no reply came back in time; Destination host unreachable is a message sent back, by a router or by your own computer, saying the packet couldn't be delivered. Firewalls often block ICMP, so a failed ping doesn't always mean a host is down.
Every IP packet has a TTL (time to live) that each router lowers by one; when it reaches zero, the router drops the packet and sends back an ICMP time exceeded message (type 11).
traceroute (tracert on Windows) uses that: it sends probes with a TTL of 1, then 2, then 3 and so on, so each router on the path reveals itself in turn, with three round-trip times per hop.
Windows tracert sends ICMP echo requests, while traceroute on macOS and Linux sends UDP probes by default. An asterisk (*) means no reply to that probe in time, which many routers do on purpose.

On Cisco IOS, ping shows ! for each reply, . for each time-out and U for unreachable; a first ping to a new neighbour often shows .!!!! while ARP completes. Ctrl+Shift+6 stops a ping or traceroute that's running.

walkthrough.title: Ping and trace a path from your own computer

steps.do: Check your computer's own network software by pinging its loopback address.
steps.code:
# Windows
ping 127.0.0.1

# macOS and Linux (-c 4 stops after four)
ping -c 4 127.0.0.1
steps.see: Replies in well under a millisecond: these packets never leave your computer.

steps.do: Ping your default gateway, your own router. ipconfig (Windows), route -n get default (macOS) or ip route (Linux) shows its address.
steps.see: Replies with small round-trip times. Use your own gateway's address, and add -c 4 on macOS and Linux.

steps.do: Ping an address on the internet. Public DNS resolvers such as 8.8.8.8 (Google Public DNS) and 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) answer pings.
steps.see: Replies with longer times than your gateway's: the packets cross many more links.

steps.do: Trace the path there. On Linux, install traceroute if it's missing (sudo apt install traceroute on Debian and Ubuntu).
steps.code:
# Windows
tracert -d 8.8.8.8

# macOS and Linux
traceroute -n 8.8.8.8
steps.see: A numbered list of hops, your router first, each with three times. Lines of * * * are routers that didn't answer; the trace usually carries on past them. -d and -n skip looking up each router's name, which is quicker.

steps.do: See what failure looks like: 192.0.2.0/24 is reserved for documentation, so nothing should answer at 192.0.2.1.
steps.see: Time-outs or an unreachable message, and a summary showing the packets were lost.

lessons.title: Checking a computer's IP settings
objectives: Find a computer's IP address, mask, default gateway and DNS servers on Windows, macOS and Linux
Recognise settings that explain a connection problem
key_points: On Windows, ipconfig shows each adapter's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, mask and default gateway; ipconfig /all adds its MAC address (Physical Address), whether DHCP is on, the DHCP server, the lease times and the DNS servers.

On Linux, ip address (or ip a) shows addresses and MAC addresses, ip route shows the routes, with the default gateway on the line starting default via, and resolvectl status shows the DNS servers on systems that use systemd-resolved.

On macOS, ifconfig shows the interfaces (en0 is usually the built-in Wi-Fi or Ethernet), ipconfig getifaddr en0 prints just the IPv4 address, netstat -rn shows the routes with the gateway on the default line, and scutil --dns lists the DNS servers.
An address starting 169.254 is link-local: Windows and macOS give themselves one when they ask for a DHCP address and get no answer, so check the cable or Wi-Fi connection and the DHCP server.
On Windows, ipconfig /release and ipconfig /renew ask DHCP for a new lease and ipconfig /flushdns empties the DNS cache; on every system, arp -a lists the IP-to-MAC mappings the computer has learned.

Settings that break connections: a gateway outside the computer's own network, a mask that doesn't match the rest of the LAN, an address another device is already using (Windows warns of a conflict), or DNS servers that don't answer.

steps.do: Windows: open Command Prompt and show the full settings of every adapter.
steps.see: For your active Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter: Physical Address, DHCP Enabled, IPv4 Address, Subnet Mask, Default Gateway, DHCP Server and DNS Servers.

steps.do: macOS: open Terminal and show the address, the default route and the DNS servers.
steps.code:
ipconfig getifaddr en0
netstat -rn -f inet | grep default
scutil --dns | grep nameserver

steps.do: Linux: open a terminal and show the addresses, the routes and the DNS servers.
steps.code:
ip -4 address show
ip route
resolvectl status

steps.do: Work out your network from your address and mask: with 192.168.1.20 and 255.255.255.0 (/24), the network is 192.168.1.0/24, and the gateway should be inside it, such as 192.168.1.1.
Look at your ARP cache: the devices on your LAN that your computer has talked to recently.
steps.see: Your gateway's IP address with its MAC address.

steps.do: Windows only, and not over a remote connection: get a fresh lease from DHCP.
steps.see: The address disappears and comes back, usually the same one, as the DHCP server renews the lease.

lab.title: Diagnose your own connection
lab.goal: Test your computer's connection layer by layer from the command line, capture the tests in Wireshark to see ICMP and TTL at work, and write a short diagnosis.
setup: Wireshark installed with permission to capture: Npcap on Windows and ChmodBPF on macOS (both offered by the installers), or membership of the wireshark group on Linux
A computer on a network you own or are allowed to test, such as your home network

steps.do: Record your settings.
steps.code:
# Windows
ipconfig /all

# macOS
ipconfig getifaddr en0
netstat -rn -f inet | grep default
scutil --dns | grep nameserver

# Linux
ip -4 address show
ip route
resolvectl status

steps.do: Start a Wireshark capture on your active interface, and type icmp in the display filter bar.
Ping your loopback address, your default gateway and 8.8.8.8, four times each (add -c 4 on macOS and Linux), using your own gateway's address.
steps.see: Replies from all three. In Wireshark, Echo (ping) request and Echo (ping) reply pairs for the gateway and 8.8.8.8, but none for 127.0.0.1, which never reaches the network interface.

steps.do: Look a name up, then trace the route to 8.8.8.8.
steps.code:
nslookup example.com

# Windows
tracert -d 8.8.8.8

# macOS and Linux
traceroute -n 8.8.8.8

steps.do: Stop the capture.
With the icmp filter on, find the Time-to-live exceeded packets. Each came from a router on the path; compare their source addresses with the hops your trace listed.
steps.see: One router for each hop that answered, in the same order as the trace.

steps.do: On Windows, select the Echo (ping) request packets your trace sent and look at Time to Live in each one's Internet Protocol header.
steps.see: 1, then 2, then 3 and so on. (On macOS and Linux the probes were UDP, so only the ICMP replies show with this filter.)

steps.do: Change the filter to dns and find your nslookup's query and its response.
steps.see: A Standard query for example.com and a Standard query response with its address.

steps.do: Write a diagnosis, one line per layer: link (connected, which interface), IP settings (address, mask, gateway, DNS), local reachability (gateway), remote reachability (8.8.8.8 and the trace) and names (nslookup). For anything that failed, say what you'd check next.

checks.text: The settings show the computer's address, mask or prefix length, and default gateway.
Pings to the loopback address, the gateway and 8.8.8.8 got replies.
The trace reached 8.8.8.8 and lists the hops on the way.
The name lookup returned an address for example.com.
The Wireshark lines show ping requests and replies and Time-to-live exceeded messages from routers on the path.
The diagnosis works through the layers, and says what to check next for anything that failed.

lab.submit: Paste your settings output; the ping, trace and nslookup output; a few lines from Wireshark's packet list (select them, right-click and choose Copy, then Summary as Text); and your layer-by-layer diagnosis. Remove anything you'd rather not share, such as your public address.
hints: If Wireshark lists no interfaces, it can't capture yet: on Windows reinstall with Npcap, on macOS run the ChmodBPF installer, and on Linux add yourself to the wireshark group and log in again.
No Time-to-live exceeded packets? Make sure the capture was running during the trace and that the filter is icmp.
Some routers are set not to answer pings: if your gateway doesn't reply but 8.8.8.8 does, the gateway is working.

project.title: Build, test and document a network, end to end
project.brief: Build a network in Packet Tracer for a small community library and prove it works from the cable up, then test and document a real network you use. In Packet Tracer, a 2911 router joins two LANs, each with a 2960 switch: a staff LAN, 192.168.10.0/24, with two PCs, and a public LAN, 192.168.20.0/24, with two PCs, a DNS server at 192.168.20.53 and a web server at 192.168.20.80. The router uses the first address on each LAN. The web server's home page names the library, and the DNS server maps www.library.test to the web server. Show that every PC can reach the web server by name, step through one page load in Simulation mode, and explain each event with the OSI and TCP/IP models. Then, on your own computer and network, record the IP settings, test the connection with ping, traceroute or tracert and nslookup, and capture the tests in Wireshark. Finish with a one-page summary comparing the two networks, and a plan for helping someone who can't open a website.
deliverables: A table of every device, port and IP address in the Packet Tracer network, with masks and gateways
ipconfig from one PC on each LAN, and the router's show ip interface brief and show ip route
Pings between the LANs, a tracert from a staff PC to the web server, and nslookup of www.library.test
A numbered list of the Simulation-mode events for one page load, each with its protocol, its layer and its purpose
Your own computer's settings, ping, trace and nslookup output, with Wireshark lines showing the ICMP traffic
A one-page summary comparing the lab network with your real one, ending with a step-by-step plan for troubleshooting a user who can't open a website

rubric.name: A working network
rubric.description: Every PC reaches the other LAN and the web server by name; addresses, masks and gateways are consistent with the plan and documented.

rubric.name: Verification
rubric.description: Ping, tracert, nslookup and show command output prove each claim and match the addressing table.

rubric.name: Layers and protocols
rubric.description: The page-load events are in the right order, and each is correctly placed in the OSI and TCP/IP models with the right transport and port (UDP 53 for DNS, TCP 80 for HTTP).

rubric.name: Real-network testing
rubric.description: The learner's own settings and tests are recorded and read correctly, with Wireshark evidence of the ICMP exchanges.

rubric.name: Summary and troubleshooting plan
rubric.description: The summary is clear and accurate, and the troubleshooting plan works through the layers in a sensible order.

project.submit: Paste your device and address table, the command output listed in the deliverables, your list of Simulation events, your Wireshark lines and your summary. A link to your .pkt file is welcome too.
